title: Marfan Syndrome
subject: Pathology
summary: Marfan syndrome is a connective‑tissue disorder caused by FBN1 mutations, leading to cystic medial necrosis of the aorta and systemic features such as tall stature and lens dislocation.

sections.p: A heritable disorder of connective tissue with aortic root dilatation, ectopia lentis, and skeletal features. Diagnosis uses the Ghent‑Nosology criteria, combining major and minor systemic signs with imaging.
b: Aortic root dilation > 2 SD for age

t.b: Measures aortic root diameter; a value >2 SD for body surface area indicates dilation and warrants surveillance
Confirms pathogenic mutation; useful when clinical criteria are equivocal
Detects lens subluxation; absence of cataract or glaucoma differentiates from homocystinuria

sections.p: Severity is staged by aortic root size and rate of growth, using the modified Ghent criteria. Staging guides timing of prophylactic surgery.
b: Stage I: Root <4.5 cm, stable growth
Stage II: Root 4.5–5.5 cm or >0.5 cm/year
Stage III: Root >5.5 cm or rapid expansion

t.b: Track growth rate; a rise >0.5 cm/year signals need for surgical review

sections.p: Primary cause is autosomal dominant FBN1 mutation. Modifier genes and environmental factors (e.g., hypertension) influence phenotype.

t.b: Elevated BP accelerates aortic dilation; control reduces risk

sections.p: Patients often present with skeletal abnormalities first, followed by cardiovascular symptoms. In low‑resource settings, chest pain or syncope may be the first clue.

t.b: Systolic murmur of aortic regurgitation; diastolic murmur of pulmonary stenosis may coexist

sections.p: Investigations focus on aortic size, valve function, and genetic confirmation. When tests are limited, clinical criteria guide management.

t.b: Aortic root >2 SD for BSA or >4.5 cm warrants surveillance

sections.p: Acute aortic dissection, sudden cardiac death, severe aortic regurgitation, and lens dislocation complications are life‑threatening.
Management is multidisciplinary: beta‑blockers or ARBs to reduce shear stress, surgical repair of the aorta when indicated, and regular surveillance.

t.b: Avoids tachycardia that worsens shear stress

sections.p: Regular echocardiograms every 6–12 months, blood pressure control, and lifestyle modifications are essential.
Homocystinuria, Ehlers‑Danlos, and Klinefelter syndrome share overlapping features but differ in genetics and management.
b: Homocystinuria – lens subluxation, marfanoid habitus, but with thrombosis and intellectual disability

sections.p: Normal aortic root size in early childhood can delay diagnosis; lens subluxation may be missed if not examined carefully.
b: Aortic root <4.5 cm in children may be normal; repeat imaging as growth occurs

whenToSeekHelp: Acute chest pain radiating to back
Rapid heart rate with new murmur

faq.q: Why is losartan used in Marfan syndrome?
faq.a: It blocks TGF‑β signalling, slowing aortic dilation and reducing dissection risk.

faq.q: Can Marfan patients have normal blood pressure?
faq.a: Yes, but uncontrolled hypertension accelerates aortic wall stress and should be treated.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of death in Marfan syndrome?
faq.a: Aortic dissection is the leading cause of mortality.

exam: A 24‑year‑old man with aortic root dilation presents with chest pain radiating to the back – what is the next step? — Immediate CT angiography to rule out dissection; if positive, emergency surgical referral.
A patient with Marfan syndrome develops sudden syncope – what red flag should prompt urgent evaluation? — New aortic regurgitation murmur or rapid heart rate; suspect dissection.

Why is beta‑blocker therapy preferred over calcium channel blockers in Marfan syndrome? — Beta‑blockers reduce heart rate and shear stress; calcium channel blockers can increase pulse pressure and worsen aortic dilation.
A 30‑year‑old woman with Marfan syndrome has a lens subluxation – which other condition must be ruled out? — Homocystinuria, as it also causes lens subluxation but has different treatment.
What is the threshold aortic root diameter that usually triggers prophylactic surgery in Marfan syndrome? — >5.5 cm or rapid growth >0.5 cm/year.

In a low‑resource setting, which test is most useful to monitor aortic size if echocardiography is unavailable? — Serial chest X‑ray with aortic root measurement, though less sensitive; use when echo cannot be done.
Why should patients with Marfan syndrome avoid strenuous activity? — It increases blood pressure and shear stress on the aortic wall, raising dissection risk.
